Solutions HW 6: NOT Collected

Loading Data and Required Packages

Run the code cells below to load required packages. We will work with the UN11 data frame from the alr4 package.

# load required packages 
library(tidyverse)
library(alr4)
library(effects)
data(UN11, package = "alr4")
glimpse(UN11)

Introduction

Load the UN11 data set from the alr4 package. The data set includes 237 observations related to national health, welfare, and education statistics for 210 places, mostly UN members, but also other areas that are not independent countries. More details can be found by running ?alr4 in the console. The variables in the data set include:

  • region: region of the world
  • group: a factor with levels oecd for countries that are members of the OECD, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, as of May 2012, africa for countries on the African continent, and other for all other countries. No OECD countries are located in Africa.
  • fertility: number of children per woman
  • ppgdp: per capita gross domestic product in US dollars
  • lifeExpF: female life expectancy, in years
  • pctUrban: percent urban

We will consider the relationship between the response log(fertility) and several of the other variables in the data set.

Question 1

Fit a linear model regressing the response log(fertility) on the predictor pctUrban. Print the estimated coefficients of the model.

Solution to Question 1

lmod <- lm(log(fertility) ~ pctUrban, data = UN11)
summary(lmod)

Call:
lm(formula = log(fertility) ~ pctUrban, data = UN11)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.87723 -0.31862  0.00894  0.29466  0.73472 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  1.500963   0.071397  21.023  < 2e-16 ***
pctUrban    -0.010163   0.001143  -8.892 3.86e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3768 on 197 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2864,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2828 
F-statistic: 79.06 on 1 and 197 DF,  p-value: 3.858e-16


Question 2

What is the equation for the fitted model?

Solution to Question 2

\[\widehat{E}(\log(\mathtt{fertility})|\mathtt{pctUrban}) = 1.5 - 0.01 \mathtt{pctUrban}\]


Question 3

Interpret the estimated coefficient for pctUrban in a straightforward sentence in the context of this example.

Solution to Question 3

The number of children per birth parent is decaying at a continuous exponential rate of 1% for each 1% increase in the percentage of the population that lives in urban regions.

For members of the United Nations, a 1% increase in the percentage of the population living in Urban regions is associated with an expected decrease in the number of children per birth parent by about 1%.


Question 4

Use the fitted model to construct an effect plot for pctUrban on fertility (on the original scale for fertility). Note you will need to modify the axes argument of the plot function.

Tip

The effects package has a vignette that may be helpful, it may be accessed by running vignette("predictor-effects-gallery", package = "effects") in the R console.

Solution to Question 4

plot(predictorEffect("pctUrban", lmod),
     axes=list(y=list(transform=exp, lab="fertility")))


Question 5

Interpret the effects plot from Question 4.

Solution to Question 5

Overall, as the percentage of the urban population increases, the average number of children a woman has tends to decrease. Have the effect seems to be weaker as percentage of the urban population increases.


Question 6

Fit the linear model regressing log(fertility) on both log(ppgdp) and lifeExpF. Print the results to the R Console. Use this fitted model to also answer Questions 7-10.

Solution to Question 6

lmod2 <- lm(log(fertility) ~ log(ppgdp) + lifeExpF, data = UN11)
summary(lmod2)

Call:
lm(formula = log(fertility) ~ log(ppgdp) + lifeExpF, data = UN11)

(Intercept)  3.50736    0.12707  27.601  < 2e-16 ***
log(ppgdp)  -0.06544    0.01781  -3.675 0.000307 ***
lifeExpF    -0.02824    0.00274 -10.306  < 2e-16 ***

Question 7

What is the equation for the fitted model from the previous Question?

Solution to Question 7

\[\widehat{E}(\log(\mathtt{fertility})|\mathtt{ppgdp}, \mathtt{lifeExpF}) = 3.5 - 0.065 \log(\mathtt{ppgdp}) - 0.03 \mathtt{lifeExpF}\]


Question 8

Mathematically, if we increase ppgdp by 25%, what is the expected decrease in fertility? (You don’t need to interpret this, just compute it).

Solution to Question 8

The mean response should change by approximately a multiplicative effect of \(\mathbf{\exp(-0.065 \log(1.25)) = 1.25^{-0.065}\approx 0.986}\). Thus, the fertility changes by about 100(0.986-1) = -1.4%.


Question 9

Interpret the estimated coefficient for ppgdp in a straightforward sentence in the context of the Question when ppgdp increases by 25%.

Solution to Question 9

For members of the United Nations, a 25% increase in the per capita gross domestic product in US dollars is associated with an expected decrease in the number of children per parent of about 1.4%, assuming average life expectancy doesn’t change.


Question 10

Construct an effect plot of ppgdp on fertility (both on their original scale) using the fitted model from Question 6.

Solution to Question 10

plot(predictorEffect("ppgdp", lmod2),
     axes=list(y=list(transform=exp, lab="fertility")))
